title: Cross-Platform Rendering Models
summary: How Flutter and React Native actually get pixels on screen, and the native/hybrid/self-rendered framing behind every cross-platform trade-off you'll be asked to reason through.

slides.markdown:
"Cross-platform" hides a real architectural split: frameworks that render UI have to decide *who actually draws the pixels* — the OS's own widget toolkit, or the framework's own engine. That single decision explains almost every practical difference between Flutter and React Native, and it's the framing every cross-platform interview question is secretly testing.

This topic gives you the three strategies, then the two concrete implementations — Flutter's engine-rendered widgets and React Native's bridge to real native views — so you can reason about performance, look-and-feel, and platform-fidelity trade-offs from mechanism, not folklore.

slides.subTitle: fully native, hybrid-native, self-rendered
slides.markdown:
Every cross-platform approach picks one of three points on this spectrum:

- **Fully native** — write once, compile to actual platform widgets on each OS (Kotlin Multiplatform with Compose/SwiftUI outputs, or simply two native codebases). Perfect fidelity, most engineering cost.
- **Hybrid-native** (React Native) — a shared logic layer drives **real native UI components** underneath. Looks and behaves exactly like a native app because it IS built from native views, just instantiated and updated from JavaScript.
- **Self-rendered** (Flutter) — the framework owns its own rendering engine and draws every pixel itself, bypassing the OS's widget toolkit entirely. Pixel-identical across platforms because nothing platform-specific is involved in drawing.

Getting this taxonomy right is the foundation for every trade-off question that follows — 'which one is faster/more native-looking/harder to update' all reduce to where on this spectrum a framework sits.

slides.sectionTitle: Why Flutter looks pixel-identical and native apps don't
slides.markdown:
A native iOS app and a native Android app rendering 'the same' button will differ — different corner radii, ripple vs highlight feedback, different default fonts — because each OS's widget toolkit has its own opinions baked in. Flutter sidesteps this entirely: it doesn't ask the OS to draw a button, it draws the button itself, pixel by pixel, using its own rendering engine. Ask it for a Material button on iOS and it draws exactly the same Material button iOS would never natively produce.

This is a genuine trade-off, not a pure win: pixel-identical also means **not automatically platform-idiomatic**. A Flutter app that never bothers to branch on platform will feel slightly 'foreign' on iOS (Android-style components) or on Android (iOS-style ones) unless the team deliberately uses Flutter's Cupertino widget set or platform-adaptive components to match each OS's real conventions.

slides.sectionTitle: Flutter's rendering engine vs React Native's native components
slides.markdown:
| | Flutter (Skia/Impeller) | React Native (native components) |
|---|---|---|
| Who draws pixels | Flutter's own engine | the OS's native rendering, same as a fully native app |
| Look and feel | consistent across platforms, opt-in platform styling | genuinely native by construction |
| New OS UI feature (e.g. a new iOS control) | Flutter has to reimplement it in Dart | often available faster via native module wrapping |
| Animation smoothness | consistent, engine-controlled | depends on which layer (JS-driven vs native-driven) animates |

Impeller, Flutter's newer rendering backend replacing Skia on some platforms, exists specifically to fix jank from runtime shader compilation that Skia suffered on first paint of certain effects — it precompiles shaders ahead of time. That detail matters if you're asked about Flutter's historical 'shader jank' complaints and whether they're still relevant.

slides.sectionTitle: The bridge boundary and where it costs performance
slides.markdown:
React Native's classic architecture runs JavaScript on its own thread, separate from the native UI thread, and every interaction between them — a JS state update triggering a native view change, a native gesture reaching JS — crosses the **bridge**: an asynchronous, batched, JSON-serializing message channel.

That serialization is the actual performance cost people mean when they say 'the bridge is slow.' It's not that JavaScript itself is slow; it's that every cross-boundary call pays a serialize/queue/deserialize tax, and a UI pattern that fires many small updates per frame (a drag gesture updating position on every touch move) can visibly lag if each update round-trips the bridge individually rather than being batched.

Flutter has no equivalent boundary for its own widgets — Dart code and the rendering engine communicate directly in-process — which is why bridge-crossing cost is specifically a React Native discussion, not a general cross-platform one.

slides.sectionTitle: The New Architecture: JSI replacing the async bridge
slides.markdown:
React Native's **New Architecture** replaces the asynchronous, JSON-serializing bridge with **JSI (JavaScript Interface)** — a mechanism letting JavaScript hold direct references to native C++ objects and call their methods **synchronously**, with no serialization step and no queue in between.

The practical upshot: interactions that used to require careful batching to avoid bridge overhead — synchronous layout measurement, gesture-driven animations — can now happen without round-tripping an async message channel at all. Fabric (the new renderer) and TurboModules (the new native module system) are both built on JSI. For an interview, the key fact isn't the acronym soup — it's that this closes much of the performance gap that used to be React Native's most-cited weakness relative to Flutter or fully native code.

"Cross-platform" markets as write-once, but real apps still need platform-specific branches for things the shared framework doesn't (and often shouldn't) abstract away: push notification setup (APNs vs FCM registration flows differ structurally), certain permission dialogs, deep platform integrations (widgets, App Clips, Android App Actions), and store-specific compliance requirements.

Teams that plan a cross-platform project assuming literally 100% shared code consistently underestimate the platform-specific 10–20% and end up scrambling near ship date. The realistic framing for planning: cross-platform shares the *bulk* of business logic and UI, not *all* of it — budget for a genuine platform-specific slice from day one rather than treating it as scope creep when it appears.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: judging performance from one janky demo
slides.markdown:
A single laggy scroll in a five-year-old React Native demo, or a Flutter app's first-launch shader-compile stutter on an old device, gets generalized into 'framework X is slow' — when the actual cause is usually a specific, fixable pattern (an unbatched bridge-heavy gesture handler, an unwarmed shader cache) rather than an inherent ceiling.

The better diagnostic instinct: profile the specific janky interaction with the framework's own tools (Flutter DevTools' performance overlay, React Native's Flipper/Perfetto traces) and identify *which layer* is the bottleneck — JS thread saturation, bridge traffic, native layout thrashing, GPU-bound drawing — before concluding anything about the framework as a whole. Frameworks evolve (New Architecture, Impeller) faster than word-of-mouth performance reputations do; citing a specific mechanism beats citing a demo you saw once.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: rendering model predicts the failure mode
slides.markdown:
A junior answer picks a framework by feature checklist. A senior answer uses the rendering model to *predict* what will go wrong before it happens: a self-rendered engine (Flutter) will struggle first with anything requiring deep, fast-moving native platform integration (a brand-new OS API on day one), because it has to be reimplemented in the framework's own terms rather than simply wrapped. A hybrid-native bridge (React Native, even post-New-Architecture) will struggle first with high-frequency, low-latency interaction loops that weren't specifically optimized for the native path.

That predictive framing is what separates 'I've used both' from 'I understand the mechanism well enough to anticipate the failure before writing the feature' — and it's exactly what [Choosing Native vs Cross-Platform](choosing-native-vs-cross-platform) turns into an actual decision framework for a real team and product.
